The ending feels entirely natural, purposeful, and earned. Throughout the story, the narrator sets up specific motifs and emotional conflicts: the "gap" between himself and the seemingly flawless Quentin, the motif of "blue ink," the narrator's foreshadowed desire to "drive home and sit on my kitchen floor for a while," the floating man in the deep end of the pool, and the three-sentence text message that ended their friendship ten years prior. 

In the final paragraphs, all of these elements converge meaningfully. Having witnessed Quentin's inability to be vulnerable, the narrator realizes that Quentin's perfection is just a defense mechanism—the same fear of "being seen mid-sentence" that the narrator suffers from. The story concludes with the narrator fulfilling the earlier foreshadowing by sitting on his kitchen floor (which he compares to the man floating in the pool) and then sending a new three-sentence message of genuine empathy to Quentin. Closing on the image of "blue ink"—now understood with compassion rather than resentment—provides a deeply satisfying resolution to the narrator's decade-long internal conflict.
